confidence_note: Study of couples by psychologist Janice Kiecolt-Glaser is cited by Maté. Exact sample size, time window and which markers fell are not verified here and are omitted; the old text's 'a few hours' is dropped. Mechanism statements (cortisol, inflammation) are Maté's general account of psychoneuroimmunology, not a claim about any one reader.
facts: Psychologist Janice Kiecolt-Glaser studied married couples.
The couples came to a research setting, were asked to discuss disagreements, and gave blood samples.

After discussions marked by hostility, measures of immune function in the blood were lower than after calmer ones; natural killer cells are among the immune measures associated with this line of research.
Maté uses this to illustrate psychoneuroimmunology: brain, nervous system and immune system share chemical messengers and are not separate.
He argues that long-lasting emotional stress keeps cortisol high and inflammation active.
He says dividing illness into mental and physical is artificial, while adding that this is not determinism.
scene_details: couples arguing while researchers take blood samples
a blood sample as the measuring tool for a quarrel
tension: An ordinary marital argument leaves a trace you can measure in the blood.
opening_idea: Open on the couples sitting down to argue in a laboratory with a blood draw.

lessons.idea: Heated conflict is a bodily event as well as an emotional one, so how you handle and recover from a quarrel matters for your body.
lessons.anchor: Immune measures lower after hostile discussions in Kiecolt-Glaser's couples.

reflect_final: After your last heated argument, what did you do with your body in the following hour, and what would you try differently next time?

use_cases.situation: You are about to start a tense conversation with your partner.
use_cases.move: Say 'I want to talk this through, but I'm too wound up; can we start in half an hour?' and walk first.

use_cases.situation: After a harsh meeting you go straight to the next task.
use_cases.move: Take five minutes away from the screen before the next call.

use_cases.situation: You explain to a friend why you stay calm after fights.
use_cases.move: Mention the couples in the lab: hostile arguments left measurable changes in immune markers.

pocket_idea: Quarrels leave a measurable mark in the blood, so give your body a real pause afterward.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Researchers took blood from arguing couples and found hostility changed immune markers.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Psychologist Kiecolt-Glaser had couples argue in a lab and drew their blood. After hostile exchanges, immune markers were lower. Gabor Maté uses it to show that mind and body are not separate.
conversation_variants.question_idea: What does your body do after a fight?
